items.short: How much water a well-watered grass field would lose in a day through evaporation and leaves, set only by the weather: sun, heat, wind and dry air. It is the starting point for any crop's water need. We compute it from NASA POWER weather.

ETc is the water your actual crop uses: ETo times the crop coefficient Kc. Kc changes with growth stage, low after planting, highest at full canopy (rice about 1.2), lower again as the crop ripens. Values come from FAO-56 tables.

Water leaving the field as vapour, from the soil surface (evaporation) and through the plants' leaves (transpiration). It is the crop's real water use, and the main way irrigation water leaves a field.

Where today's soil moisture ranks against the same time of year in other years. 50 is typical; 20 means drier than 80% of years; 90 means wetter than 90% of years. Ours comes from NASA SMAP for the top metre of soil over a 9 km area.

A satellite measure of how green and leafy the ground is, from 0 (bare soil or water, sometimes below 0) to about 0.9 (dense healthy crop). It rises as a crop grows and drops at harvest. We read it from NASA HLS, Landsat and Sentinel-2.

Our field calendar sorts each day into bare (NDVI below 0.20), partial cover (0.20 to 0.35), covered (above 0.35) or water. These cut-offs are a rule of thumb, not tuned to your field; bare soil in winter is when rain can wash soil away.

A frost night here is one where the air temperature falls to 32 F (0 C) or below; a hard frost is 28 F (-2 C) or below. Low spots and calm, clear nights frost first, so your field can be colder than the weather station.

Days when the daily high reaches 104 F (40 C) or more, which stresses most crops and livestock. We also count heat waves: three or more days in a row at 95 F (35 C) or above. NASA POWER runs warmer than local stations in summer, so we show both.

Crop water use (ETc) minus the rain that soaks into the root zone is roughly what irrigation must supply. Irrigation need is that shortfall divided by how efficiently water is delivered. It is an estimate for planning, not a schedule.

An acre-foot is the water that covers one acre one foot deep: about 326,000 gallons. One acre-foot per acre equals 12 inches, or 305 mm, of water over the field. So 1,000 mm of crop water use is about 3.3 acre-feet per acre.

NASA's GRACE and GRACE-FO satellites sense tiny changes in Earth's gravity caused by water stored underground. A model turns this into a groundwater percentile for an area about 25 km across: below 30 is low for the time of year, 50 typical.

California's Sustainable Groundwater Management Act (2014). Local groundwater agencies must bring basins into balance, which can mean pumping limits or fees. Check your local agency's plan before counting on well water for a new rotation.

Each satellite value covers an area, its footprint. HLS greenness is 30 m (one field has hundreds of pixels); SMAP soil moisture is 9 km and GRACE groundwater about 25 km, so those describe your area, not your field alone.

A public service that estimates actual crop water use from satellite images (Landsat) with several models and averages them. We use it to check our crop water numbers against measured use on your field, never to set the scores.

The rule detector labels each satellite date with fixed greenness and water cut-offs. The machine-learning detector (a random forest) learns the labels from nearby fields with known crops. Where they agree you can trust the calendar more; where they differ, check locally.

NASA's GPM IMERG estimates rain every half hour worldwide from a constellation of satellites; we use the daily total for the 10 km square over your field. At these fields it reads wetter than the nearest rain gauges, so we show both.

NASA's OPERA project maps open and shallow water at 30 m from each Landsat and Sentinel-2 pass. We count how much of your field was under water on each clear day, which shows winter flooding and floods.

note: Plain-language definitions (<= 60 words, one source each). Thresholds quoted are the ones this app uses.
